real_title: Forthwell Limited v Pontegadea UK Limited
appeal_from: Court of Session, Inner House, First Division (Scotland) [2024] CSIH 38; 2025 SC 127
facts: The Landlord and the Tenant are, respectively, landlord and tenant of restaurant premises in Glasgow under a lease dated 1996. Neither was an original party to the lease; the tenant's interest was assigned to the Tenant in 2013. The Tenant granted its wholly-owned subsidiary (the Subsidiary) a licence to occupy, and the Subsidiary traded from the premises as a restaurant. The Tenant does not aver that the Landlord knew of the licence. The licence provides that the Subsidiary cannot oblige the Tenant to carry out repairs and that the Tenant is not liable to the Subsidiary for loss from any deficiency in the premises. The lease prohibits sub-letting and parting with or sharing possession, requires the Landlord to rebuild parts damaged by insured risks including flooding, and the Tenant avers an implied term that the Landlord will repair the common parts. In December 2020 and January 2021 the premises suffered flooding and water ingress, and a fire followed the first flood. Repairs have not been carried out and the restaurant has been unable to reopen. The Tenant sued the Landlord in the Court of Session (commercial action) for specific implement of the repairing obligations, damages, damages for breach of the common parts obligation, and professional fees. Those claims require proof. The Tenant also sued, on behalf of the Subsidiary, for the Subsidiary's past and future loss of profits. These are the Subsidiary's own losses, not losses the Tenant suffered in its own performance interest. The Tenant accepts it cannot bring the claim within the narrow Albazero ground or the broader St Martins ground, and relies solely on a solution proposed by Lord Clyde in Panatown and adopted for Scots law by Lord Drummond Young in McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton. The Landlord challenged the relevancy of the transferred loss claims. The commercial judge allowed them to proceed to proof before answer. The Landlord reclaimed, and by majority the First Division allowed the reclaiming motion and dismissed the transferred loss claims. The Tenant appeals to the Supreme Court. A separate argument about mutual insurance was rejected below and is not appealed.

issues.question: Does Scots law permit a contracting party to recover, on behalf of a third party and as a matter of general legal policy, the third party's loss caused by a breach of contract, in circumstances falling outside the narrow Albazero ground and the broader St Martins ground (the Panatown/Lord Clyde solution)?
On the pleaded facts, is the Tenant entitled to recover the Subsidiary's loss of profits from the Landlord as transferred loss?

appellant_submissions: The Tenant submits that its transferred loss claims rest solely on Lord Clyde's solution in Panatown, which Lord Drummond Young considered to be part of Scots law in McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton. It says the court should endorse that approach. It points out that the approach was followed in Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair and in Axon Well, and that the commercial judge and Lord Malcolm (dissenting in the First Division) accepted it. It argues the approach is a just solution and accords with fundamental principles of Scots law, which has no doctrine of consideration, has long recognised third party rights, and need not align with English law on privity. Under that approach the law deems the contracting party to claim on behalf of itself and others who have suffered loss, so that no loss caused by a breach goes uncompensated (a legal black hole). The contracting party must account to the third party for what it recovers. The Tenant submits that such a claim should be available only where the contracting party has a material interest in the loss suffered by the third party, for example in family or corporate groups. It says that requirement is a robust limiting factor and that the ordinary rules on remoteness and reasonableness of damages would also apply. It says it has a material interest in the Subsidiary's losses, that the Subsidiary was closely connected with the lease, and that the Landlord must have contemplated that the restaurant trader would lose profits if the repairing obligations were breached.
respondent_submissions: The Landlord submits that a contracting party can ordinarily recover damages only for its own loss, and that the transferred loss claims are ill-founded in law and should be dismissed. It says the claims are for the Subsidiary's consequential losses and are not losses suffered by the Tenant in its performance interest. It argues that Lord Clyde's solution in Panatown was not adopted by the other members of the House of Lords, was obiter, and is inconsistent with their reasoning. It also argues that later authority (Swynson, and BV Nederlandse Industrie in the Court of Appeal) treats transferred loss as a limited exception grounded in the intention of the contracting parties and driven by legal necessity. The Landlord relies on the First Division majority's view that the Tenant had not sustained the claimed losses and that, even if the narrow or broader exceptions applied in Scots law, the pleaded case did not meet their criteria. It points to the absence of any common contractual intention to benefit the Subsidiary, to the licence terms under which the Tenant would not be liable to account to the Subsidiary, and to the lease prohibition on sub-letting and sharing possession. It says Lord Drummond Young's obiter formulation lacks authority.
legal_materials: Albacruz v Albazero [1977] AC 774 (narrow ground: contemplated transfer of proprietary interest, no direct remedy for the third party). Linden Gardens Trust v Lenesta Sludge Disposals; St Martins Property Corpn v Sir Robert McAlpine [1994] 1 AC 85 (Lord Griffiths, broader ground based on the contracting party's performance interest). Alfred McAlpine Construction v Panatown [2001] 1 AC 518 (Lord Clyde's proposed solution; Lord Goff and Lord Millett favouring the broader ground; a direct remedy for the third party in that case). Swynson v Lowick Rose [2017] UKSC 32; [2018] AC 313 (transferred loss as an exception to the general rule that a claimant recovers only its own loss). BV Nederlandse Industrie van Eiprodukten v Rembrandt Enterprises [2019] EWCA Civ 596. McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton v Abercromby Motor Group 2003 SCLR 323. Marquess of Aberdeen and Temair v Turcan Connell [2008] CSOH 183. Axon Well Intervention Products v Craig [2015] CSOH 4. Dunlop v Lambert (1839) 6 Cl & Fin 600. Contracts (Third Party Rights) (Scotland) Act 2017; Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. Lease clauses 5.2.2, 5.3.2, 5.3.3.1, 13.2; Licence clause 8.
actual_reasoning_summary: The Supreme Court held that Lord Clyde's Panatown solution was not endorsed by any other member of the House of Lords, does not represent the law of England and Wales, and is contrary to Swynson, where the exception rests on the contracting parties' intention rather than a rule of law. Lord Drummond Young's adoption of it in McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton was therefore based on an error. The proposed exception is also too wide, because it allows recovery where the third party was not within the parties' contemplation at contracting, and too indefinite, because the limits of the 'material interest' test are vague. The Court saw no cogent case for the exception, noting the third party rights legislation and that legal black holes are rare. The outcome is not unjust, since the Tenant and the Subsidiary chose their corporate structure and the licence appears to breach the lease. The First Division was correct. The Court also observed that the narrow Albazero exception is part of Scots law, and left open whether the broader ground is part of English or Scots law.
outcome_evidence: Para 44: "For these reasons the First Division was correct to allow the reclaiming motion. I would dismiss the appeal." Para 1: Lord Doherty gives the judgment, with which Lord Reed, Lord Stephens, Lady Simler and Lord Hodge agree. Para 3: counsel agreed that "if it is unsuccessful the appeal should be dismissed."
